data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a non-inductive, pragmatic rule of action: we prefer the theory that has survived severe tests not because it is likely true, but because it is the best available instrument for avoiding known errors in immediate decision-making.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent requires a probability estimate to make any decision (e.g., in risk assessment involving lives).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'avoiding known errors' implicitly assumes that the future will resemble the past regarding which errors are relevant.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's own advice to 'act on the best tested theory' cannot be distinguished from 'act on the most probable theory' in practical outcomes.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Pragmatic Instrumentalism: Corroboration reports past performance without projecting future success probabilistically. The preference is rational because acting on a falsified theory guarantees error, while acting on an unfalsified one leaves open the possibility of success. This is a logical asymmetry, not an inductive inference.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
